This looks like researching objects, people and places, and figuring out how those stories come together in a way that makes sense – and feels meaningful - to visitors.\n\nShe’s currently helping develop both long-term and temporary exhibitions for our opening, alongside designers, community members and colleagues across the rohe, while also shaping the collections going forward - from what gets added to how it’s cared for and shared in future exhibitions.\n\nSarah loves how many different roles come together to make a museum work. Curator is just one part of it; it takes a mix of people and skills to bring everything to life (and some days it feels a bit like you get to play Indiana Jones!).\n\nOutside of work, she’s a self-confessed homebody. Cross stitching on the couch with her cat Koi, drying flowers, working on her family tree, and heading out to explore Southland’s heritage spots with her partner. She also plays a questionable amount of online Scrabble and is an overachiever at online shopping… purely in support of the local post industry, of course.\n\nKā mihi nui, Sarah. We’re so lucky to have you as part of the team at Te Unua.\n\n\n📸 'Oscar' the ventriloquist dummy, 1930s. Collection of Te Kupeka Tiaki Taoka Southern Regional Collections Trust, 83.3223.1.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_i-feel-very-very-lucky-that-i-get-to-do-activity-7477556993268879360-NWD0"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Invercargill City Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/invercargill-city-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-21T22:05:25.357Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_a-huge-congratulations-to-bill-mclean-linda-activity-7474583281590738944-h9vc","text":"A huge congratulations to Bill McLean, Linda Te Au, and Ngarita Te Patu, who took home the Services to Sport Awards at the ILT Southland Murihiku Sports Awards last week.\n \nWe're proud to sponsor this category, which recognises the incredible people who have given so much back to Southland through their sports.\n \nLinda Te Au was recognised for her tireless volunteer work with Southland Harriers and Athletics Southland.\n \nNgarita Te Patu was honoured for her unwavering contribution to BMX in Southland over many years and for playing a vital role in the development of the world-class facility on Elizabeth Street.\n \n Bill McLean was recognised for his lifetime contribution to football in Southland.\n \nA huge congratulations to all the winners and nominees. It's inspiring to see the talent, passion, and dedication that make sport such an important part of our region.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_a-huge-congratulations-to-bill-mclean-linda-activity-7474583281590738944-h9vc"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Invercargill City Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/invercargill-city-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-11T03:33:47.979Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_a-unique-hospitality-opportunity-is-now-available-activity-7470679653863587840-z8nL","text":"A unique hospitality opportunity is now available within one of Southland's most significant new developments.\n\nExpressions of Interest are open for the café tenancy at Te Unua Museum of Southland, a new museum and landmark cultural destination currently under development in Invercargill.\n \nFor the right operator, this represents a rare opportunity to be part of a landmark project from day one.\n \nVisit our website for more information. Expressions of Interest are open until 5pm on Wednesday 8 July 2026: https://www.teunua.nz/cafe","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_a-unique-hospitality-opportunity-is-now-available-activity-7470679653863587840-z8nL"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Invercargill City Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/invercargill-city-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-10T20:23:17.319Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_museums-are-full-of-stories-and-david-dudfield-activity-7470571312227315713-6sI4","text":"Museums are full of stories, and David Dudfield helps bring them to life at Te Unua.\n\nDavid has been part of our Museum team since 2008 (aside from a short adventure elsewhere along the way). Today, he’s Team Leader – Experience.\n\nFor David, the goal isn’t just for visitors to look at old things, but instead immerse themselves in stories.\n\nBehind every exhibition is a team of curators, designers, preparators and educators working together. Curators act like history detectives, uncovering the stories behind objects. Designers and preparators transform those discoveries into exhibitions, while the education team helps bring it all to life for school groups. David’s role is making sure all those moving pieces come together so every visitor has a great experience.\n\nHis interest in history started early. David grew up in Orepuki near Monkey Island and Gemstone Beach. What might look like a quiet coastal spot today has layers of fascinating history, from places of deep cultural significance for mana whenua to the remains of large-scale mining.\n\nAs a kid he loved local history books and learning about how the land - and the people - have shaped Southland’s landscape and stories over time.\n\nThe most rewarding part of his job? Seeing visitors genuinely connect with an exhibition or programme.\n\nOutside of the museum, David keeps busy walking his dog, watching cheesy horror movies with his family, gaming, photography, music and playing in bands - plus the occasional deep dive into other corners of Southland’s history.\n\nHis controversial food opinion? The humble Belgian biscuit is the undisputed king of café sweet treats \n\nKā mihi nui, Davey. Thanks for being such an important part of the team at Te Unua Museum of Southland.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_museums-are-full-of-stories-and-david-dudfield-activity-7470571312227315713-6sI4"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Invercargill City Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/invercargill-city-council"},"datePublished":"2026-05-28T01:49:49.710Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_we-hosted-travel-agents-in-invercargill-this-activity-7465580058569568256-2npT","text":"We hosted travel agents in Invercargill this week, showcasing three of our key local experiences: Te Unua Museum of Southland, Queens Park, and Te Moutere - Tuatara Island, as part of the 2026 Great South Murihiku Post TRENZ Famil.\n\nAt Te Unua, the group got a behind-the-scenes look at what’s coming as the museum redevelopment takes shape. It gave agents a clear sense of how Murihiku Southland’s stories are being brought to life in a modern, more engaging way - and why this will be a major draw card for future visitors.\nThe group also explored Queens Park and visited Te Moutere - Tuatara Island (in the Queens Park animal reserve), home to Henry the Tuatara. Together, the experience highlighted the unique mix of nature, wildlife, and accessible green spaces that make Queens Park such an important part of the Invercargill visitor experience.\nThese experiences show what Invercargill does well: accessible, high-quality visitor experiences that are deeply tied to place and story. For agents, it reinforces the city as a meaningful part of a wider Southland journey, and a must-stop destination in its own right.\nKa pai to our fantastic staff for opening the doors and showcasing these Invercargill assets so strongly - balancing future-focused development with care for our taoka and treasured landmarks. ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_we-hosted-travel-agents-in-invercargill-this-activity-7465580058569568256-2npT"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Invercargill City Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/invercargill-city-council"},"datePublished":"2026-05-22T21:00:03.392Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/invercargill-city-council_public-pools-are-often-viewed-simply-as-recreational-activity-7463695195746791424-LqBZ","text":"Public pools are often viewed simply as recreational facilities.\n\nIn reality, they are some of the most important pieces of social infrastructure a community can have.\n\nThis week we’re recognising our Pool Manager, Stephen Cook for 21 years of service at Splash Palace, alongside 28 years working within the aquatics industry.\n\nAcross more than two decades at Splash Palace, he has helped guide the facility through major operational growth and change. From infrastructure upgrades and increasing participation demand, to sector leadership work across water treatment, disability and inclusion, Poolsafe assessment, and regional aquatic training initiatives.\n\nWhen he first returned to Splash Palace in 2005, annual participation sat at approximately 305,000 visits. In 2025/26, the facility is tracking toward almost 400,000 annual visits, reflecting both growing demand and the important role aquatic facilities continue to play in community wellbeing.\n\nWhat stands out most is his perspective on the role facilities like Splash Palace play:\n\n“Splash Palace is not simply a leisure facility, it is vital community hub that improves health outcomes, builds community connection, supports economic activity and delivers lifelong water safety and wellbeing benefits for the community.”\n\nIn an industry where community facilities are under increasing pressure, long-term leadership and institutional knowledge matter. The impact of that experience is often invisible to the public - seen instead in safe operations, strong community trust, staff development, and the thousands of everyday interactions that make people feel welcome in a public space.\n\nThank you, Steve, for the leadership, expertise and commitment you’ve brought not only to Splash Palace, but to the wider aquatics sector and Southland community over the past 21         " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">“I feel very, very lucky that I get to do a job I genuinely love.”

Sarah Robinson was nine years old when she watched a documentary on ancient Egyptian mummies - and she was instantly hooked.

Now, she’s Senior Curator at Te Unua Museum of Southland, working on exhibitions that share precious stories from across Murihiku Southland.

A lot of her role involves working with the vast collections you will see on display at Te Unua. This looks like researching objects, people and places, and figuring out how those stories come together in a way that makes sense – and feels meaningful - to visitors.

She’s currently helping develop both long-term and temporary exhibitions for our opening, alongside designers, community members and colleagues across the rohe, while also shaping the collections going forward - from what gets added to how it’s cared for and shared in future exhibitions.

Sarah loves how many different roles come together to make a museum work. Curator is just one part of it; it takes a mix of people and skills to bring everything to life (and some days it feels a bit like you get to play Indiana Jones!).

Outside of work, she’s a self-confessed homebody. Cross stitching on the couch with her cat Koi, drying flowers, working on her family tree, and heading out to explore Southland’s heritage spots with her partner. She also plays a questionable amount of online Scrabble and is an overachiever at online shopping… purely in support of the local post industry, of course.

Kā mihi nui, Sarah. We’re so lucky to have you as part of the team at Te Unua.


📸 'Oscar' the ventriloquist dummy, 1930s. Collection of Te Kupeka Tiaki Taoka Southern Regional Collections Trust, 83.3223.1.</p>

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Museums are full of stories, and David Dudfield helps bring them to life at Te Unua.

David has been part of our Museum team since 2008 (aside from a short adventure elsewhere along the way). Today, he’s Team Leader – Experience.

For David, the goal isn’t just for visitors to look at old things, but instead immerse themselves in stories.

Behind every exhibition is a team of curators, designers, preparators and educators working together. Curators act like history detectives, uncovering the stories behind objects. Designers and preparators transform those discoveries into exhibitions, while the education team helps bring it all to life for school groups. David’s role is making sure all those moving pieces come together so every visitor has a great experience.

His interest in history started early. David grew up in Orepuki near Monkey Island and Gemstone Beach. What might look like a quiet coastal spot today has layers of fascinating history, from places of deep cultural significance for mana whenua to the remains of large-scale mining.

As a kid he loved local history books and learning about how the land - and the people - have shaped Southland’s landscape and stories over time.

The most rewarding part of his job? Seeing visitors genuinely connect with an exhibition or programme.

Outside of the museum, David keeps busy walking his dog, watching cheesy horror movies with his family, gaming, photography, music and playing in bands - plus the occasional deep dive into other corners of Southland’s history.

His controversial food opinion? The humble Belgian biscuit is the undisputed king of café sweet treats 

Kā mihi nui, Davey. Thanks for being such an important part of the team at Te Unua Museum of Southland.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We hosted travel agents in Invercargill this week, showcasing three of our key local experiences: Te Unua Museum of Southland, Queens Park, and Te Moutere - Tuatara Island, as part of the 2026 <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/great-southnz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Great South</a> Murihiku Post TRENZ Famil.

At Te Unua, the group got a behind-the-scenes look at what’s coming as the museum redevelopment takes shape. It gave agents a clear sense of how Murihiku Southland’s stories are being brought to life in a modern, more engaging way - and why this will be a major draw card for future visitors.
The group also explored Queens Park and visited Te Moutere - Tuatara Island (in the Queens Park animal reserve), home to Henry the Tuatara. Together, the experience highlighted the unique mix of nature, wildlife, and accessible green spaces that make Queens Park such an important part of the Invercargill visitor experience.
These experiences show what Invercargill does well: accessible, high-quality visitor experiences that are deeply tied to place and story. For agents, it reinforces the city as a meaningful part of a wider Southland journey, and a must-stop destination in its own right.
Ka pai to our fantastic staff for opening the doors and showcasing these Invercargill assets so strongly - balancing future-focused development with care for our taoka and treasured landmarks. </p>

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Public pools are often viewed simply as recreational facilities.

In reality, they are some of the most important pieces of social infrastructure a community can have.

This week we’re recognising our Pool Manager, <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/stephen-cook-b370a8224?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Stephen Cook</a> for 21 years of service at Splash Palace, alongside 28 years working within the aquatics industry.

Across more than two decades at Splash Palace, he has helped guide the facility through major operational growth and change. From infrastructure upgrades and increasing participation demand, to sector leadership work across water treatment, disability and inclusion, Poolsafe assessment, and regional aquatic training initiatives.

When he first returned to Splash Palace in 2005, annual participation sat at approximately 305,000 visits. In 2025/26, the facility is tracking toward almost 400,000 annual visits, reflecting both growing demand and the important role aquatic facilities continue to play in community wellbeing.

What stands out most is his perspective on the role facilities like Splash Palace play:

“Splash Palace is not simply a leisure facility, it is vital community hub that improves health outcomes, builds community connection, supports economic activity and delivers lifelong water safety and wellbeing benefits for the community.”

In an industry where community facilities are under increasing pressure, long-term leadership and institutional knowledge matter. The impact of that experience is often invisible to the public - seen instead in safe operations, strong community trust, staff development, and the thousands of everyday interactions that make people feel welcome in a public space.

Thank you, Steve, for the leadership, expertise and commitment you’ve brought not only to Splash Palace, but to the wider aquatics sector and Southland community over the past 21 years.</p>

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">While the physical build of Te Unua Museum of Southland is scheduled to be completed later this year, an enormous amount of work is also happening behind the scenes alongside our community to help shape the stories, experiences, and narratives that will live within the museum.

Recently, members of the Marching Southland Hokonui Under-18 marching team joined us at Anderson House to help film part of an experience that will feature within Te Unua.

For many Southlanders, marching represents generations of commitment, teamwork, pride, and community connection - with strong ties to families and communities right across Murihiku.

That connection to Southland’s identity is exactly why we wanted marching reflected within the museum.

The Hokonui team brought incredible energy to the filming, performing their routine time and time again throughout the day with absolute precision and pride.

There’s a huge amount of mahi happening behind the scenes to help bring these experiences to life, and it’s pretty special seeing local groups helping shape how the stories of Murihiku will be shared for future generations.

Visit <a class="link" href="http://teunua.nz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>teunua.nz</a> to read the full story 👉 <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/eKQHvttf?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/eKQHvttf</a></p>
